implementation_notes: There is no rate limiter in the C++ standard library, so the classic structure is written by hand around std::chrono::steady_clock - the monotonic clock cppreference describes as most suitable for measuring intervals - with a std::mutex and a token count refilled by elapsed time. Two call shapes fall out: a non-blocking try_acquire that refuses and lets the caller answer 429 or back-pressure, and a blocking acquire that waits on a condition variable until the deficit clears. For asynchronous I/O stacks the same policy is realized with Boost.Asio timers instead (see the sibling variant); the blocking class remains justified when the limiter is shared by threads rather than by completion handlers.
pitfalls: std::chrono::system_clock is not monotonic; refills computed from it jump when the wall clock is stepped.
Tokens must be capped at the burst size after every refill, otherwise an idle bucket accumulates unbounded credit.
A blocking acquire on a condition variable must re-check its predicate and recompute the refill after every wake-up, including spurious ones.
Floating-point token counts under heavy contention accumulate drift; integer tokens with a fixed refill tick avoid it.

variants.name: Boost.Asio steady_timer pacing
variants.implementation_notes: In an asynchronous client the limiter is a timer rather than a counter: before issuing a request to a quota'd dependency, expires_after the remaining interval and async_wait, then resume from the completion handler on the io_context. The timer runs on the same steady_clock basis, so the pacing is immune to wall-clock steps; the Boost docs note that changing an active timer's expiry cancels pending waits and that the handler then observes operation_aborted, which matters when the wait is re-armed from inside the handler.
pitfalls: Re-arming the timer cancels pending waits and surfaces operation_aborted in the old handler; treating every error as fatal drops the pacing loop.
Blocking inside the completion handler stalls the io_context thread and destroys the rate control it was meant to enforce.
